sections.title: Checking the step-size endpoints in Lean
sections.intro: These final proofs check the assumptions of a concrete quadratic and then show why the two strict step-size endpoints cannot be included. They also provide short examples of differentiating, rewriting, induction, and contradiction. All snippets below come from \lean{Sharpness.lean}.

blocks.title: Define the model objective
blocks.explanation: The definition is $F(x)=x^2/2$ on the real line. We use $F$ for this objective here so that it is distinguished from the arbitrary $f$ in the main theorem.

blocks.title: Compute the scalar derivative
blocks.explanation:
\lean{hasDerivAt_id x} states that the identity map has derivative $1$ at $x$. The method \lean{.pow 2} differentiates its square, and \lean{.div_const 2} divides the derivative by $2$. Thus the stored fact \lean{h} has derivative $(2x)/2$, while the goal requests derivative $x$. \lean{convert h using 1} leaves two matching obligations. The function equality is definitional and is closed by \lean{rfl}; \lean{simp} reduces $(2x)/2$ to $x$. After this block,
\[
\operatorname{HasDerivAt}(F,x,x),\qquad F'(x)=x.
\]

blocks.title: Obtain differentiability everywhere
blocks.explanation: For each real $x$, the derivative fact just proved supplies differentiability at $x$ through \lean{.differentiableAt}. The function \lean{fun x => ...} supplies this fact for every point, which is the meaning of \lean{Differentiable}.

blocks.title: Identify the real gradient
blocks.explanation:
For a real-valued function on the real line, \lean{gradient_eq_deriv'} identifies its gradient with its scalar derivative. The second rewrite uses \lean{(quadratic_hasDerivAt x).deriv} to conclude
\[
\nabla F(x)=\operatorname{deriv}F(x)=x.
\]
The \lean{@[simp]} attribute registers this equality as a simplification rule for later proofs.

blocks.title: Reduce strong convexity to convexity of the adjusted function
blocks.explanation:
The goal is $1$-strong convexity. The reverse implication \lean{.mpr} of the equivalence changes the task to convexity of
\[
x\longmapsto F(x)-\frac12\norm x^2.
\]
The local equality \lean{hzero} will identify this entire function with the constant zero function.

blocks.title: Prove that the adjusted function vanishes
blocks.explanation:
\lean{funext x} reduces equality of the two functions to equality of their values at an arbitrary $x$. The simplifications unfold $F$, replace the real norm by $|x|$, and use $|x|^2=x^2$. The remaining scalar identity is
\[
\frac{x^2}{2}-\frac12x^2=0,
\]
which \lean{ring} proves by polynomial normalization. This establishes \lean{hzero}.

blocks.title: Finish strong convexity
blocks.explanation: Rewriting by \lean{hzero} makes the convexity goal a statement about the constant zero function. \lean{convexOn_const} supplies its convexity on the convex domain \lean{Set.univ}. Together with the previous equivalence, this proves that $F$ is $1$-strongly convex.

blocks.title: Check the gradient Lipschitz constant
blocks.explanation:
The embedded \lean{show} proves the equality of vector fields $\nabla F=\operatorname{id}$ by function extensionality and \lean{gradient_quadratic}. The library fact \lean{LipschitzWith.id} is the inequality
\[
|\operatorname{id}(x)-\operatorname{id}(y)|\le1\,|x-y|.
\]
\lean{simpa only} substitutes the field equality into this fact. Thus all function assumptions of the convergence theorem hold with $m=L=1$.

blocks.title: State the exact iterates and prove the base case
blocks.explanation: The claim is $x_n=(1-\alpha)^n$ for the initial point $x_0=1$. \lean{induction n with} gives a base goal and an induction step. In the zero case, the defining equation of \lean{iterate} and the rule $a^0=1$ reduce both sides to $1$, so \lean{simp} closes that goal.

blocks.title: Perform the induction step
blocks.explanation:
The induction hypothesis is $x_n=(1-\alpha)^n$. The rewrites unfold the successor iteration, substitute this hypothesis, replace the gradient by the identity, express real scalar multiplication as multiplication, and expand the successor power. The resulting identity is
\[
(1-\alpha)^n-\alpha(1-\alpha)^n=(1-\alpha)^n(1-\alpha),
\]
which \lean{ring} proves. Therefore the exact formula holds for every real step $\alpha$ and every $n$.

blocks.title: Evaluate the two boundary sequences
blocks.explanation:
With $\alpha=0$, the formula is $(1-0)^n=1$; \lean{simp} proves the first lemma. With $\alpha=2$, it is $(1-2)^n=(-1)^n$; \lean{norm_num} evaluates the constant subtraction. These establish
\[
x_n=1\quad(\alpha=0),\qquad x_n=(-1)^n\quad(\alpha=2).
\]

blocks.title: Assume convergence at zero step and identify the constant sequence
blocks.explanation:
The theorem states the negation of convergence to $0$. \lean{intro h} assumes that convergence in order to derive a contradiction. The \lean{change ... at h} command presents the sequence explicitly as a function of $n$. The exact formula \lean{quadratic_iterate_zero} then turns \lean{h} into the named limit fact
\[
\texttt{hn}:\quad (n\mapsto1)\longrightarrow0.
\]
Here $0$ is the minimizer because $F(0)=0\le F(x)$, with equality only at $x=0$.

blocks.title: Use uniqueness of limits to obtain a contradiction
blocks.explanation: The constant sequence $1$ tends to $1$, by \lean{tendsto_const_nhds}. Together with \lean{hn}, uniqueness of limits in the real line gives $1=0$, stored as \lean{heq}. \lean{norm_num at heq} evaluates that impossible equality and closes the contradiction. Thus the lower endpoint cannot be part of the universal convergence guarantee.

blocks.title: Assume convergence at the upper endpoint and take norms
blocks.explanation:
Again \lean{intro h} assumes convergence to zero. Applying \lean{h.norm} gives $|x_n|\to|0|$. The simplifications use $x_n=(-1)^n$, $|a^n|=|a|^n$, $|-1|=1$, and $1^n=1$, yielding
\[
\texttt{hn}:\quad(n\mapsto1)\longrightarrow0.
\]
This is the exact reason an oscillating sequence cannot converge to zero.

blocks.title: Contradict uniqueness of limits again
blocks.explanation: The constant norm sequence also tends to $1$, so \lean{tendsto_nhds_unique} produces $1=0$ and \lean{norm_num} eliminates it. This proves failure at $\alpha=2=2/L$ for a function satisfying all the hypotheses with $m=L=1$.
